strengths: Principled mathematical derivation: The use of orthogonal basis properties (Hermite polynomials under Gaussian distribution and Fourier series under uniform distribution) to compute exact second-order moments and equate forward and backward gains provides an elegant, closed-form variance-preserving initialization scheme.

Meaningful benchmark tasks: Unlike many recent works on learnable activations and KANs that restrict evaluation to synthetic functions or MNIST, this work evaluates on standard large-scale benchmarks: ImageNet-1K with ConvNeXt-T and OpenWebText language modeling with GPT-2.

Careful implementation considerations: The paper provides concrete details on numerical stability (e.g., using log-gamma to compute coefficients, recurrence relations to avoid O(d^2) explicit polynomial expansion, and CUDA kernel algorithms).
weaknesses: Overclaiming theoretical contributions: Bullet 3 of the contributions and Proposition 3.32 claim 'proving that polynomially activated deep neural networks are polynomial mappings' as a primary contribution. Compositions and linear combinations of polynomials trivially form a polynomial; this is standard algebra and should not be framed as a novel theoretical finding.

Incomplete theoretical treatment for tropical activations: While Hermite and Fourier activations have rigorous variance-preserving derivations, tropical polynomial activations lack this foundation (as noted in Remark 3.29, where initialization is set to all ones and variance analysis is deferred). Grouping tropical activations into the core variance-preservation narrative feels disjointed.

Absence of wall-clock latency and throughput benchmarks: Although theoretical FLOPs and parameter overheads are discussed, learnable activations typically suffer from significant memory-bandwidth and kernel launch overhead compared to highly optimized activations (e.g., fused GELU or SwiGLU). Empirical wall-clock training/inference speeds across batches should be reported.

Marginal empirical improvements and lack of error bars: On ImageNet-1K, Hermite degree 3 achieves 82.34% vs. the GELU baseline of 82.04% (+0.3%), while Fourier achieves 81.91% (worse than baseline). Without multiple seeds and standard deviations, it is difficult to determine whether these modest gains are statistically significant.

Missing modern baselines: The comparison is restricted solely to standard static GELU. Comparing against contemporary parameterized/gated activations (such as SwiGLU) or other modern learnable activation methods (e.g., Padé Activation Units / PAU) would provide a fairer and more comprehensive assessment.

strengths: Principled initialization analysis: The paper addresses the well-known instability of polynomial activations by deriving closed-form forward and backward variance-preserving gains using the orthonormality of Hermite and Fourier bases.

Evaluation beyond toy tasks: Unlike many prior polynomial/KAN-style activation works that only evaluate on MNIST or low-dimensional synthetic benchmarks, this paper evaluates on standard large-scale benchmarks (ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1K and GPT-2 124M on OpenWebText).

Comprehensive ablations: The ablation studies systematically assess the impact of polynomial degree, the proposed initialization vs. GELU-fitting, and coefficient learnability, clearly confirming the benefit of the proposed initialization scheme for Hermite polynomials.
weaknesses: Missing runtime and throughput benchmarks: Although Section 4.3 theoretically analyzes parameter counts and algorithmic complexity ($O(d)$ vs. $O(d^2)$), the paper lacks empirical wall-clock training times, inference latencies, and throughput (tokens/sec or images/sec) compared to highly optimized baseline kernels (e.g., fused GELU/SiLU).

Overstated theoretical novelty of Proposition 3.32: Proposition 3.32 and Corollary D.1 formally prove that composing degree-$d$ polynomial layers yields a degree-$d^L$ polynomial mapping. This is an elementary algebraic fact and well known in the polynomial neural network literature (e.g., Kileel et al., 2019; Chrysos et al., 2020), so framing it as a primary contribution is overstated.

Disconnection and heuristic treatment of tropical activations: While Hermite and Fourier activations are grounded in variance preservation, tropical activations do not share this theoretical framework (as noted in Remark 3.29, where initialization is purely heuristic 'all ones'). This weakens the thematic cohesion of the proposed method.

Marginal empirical gains and lack of statistical significance: The improvements on ImageNet-1k (+0.30% top-1 for Hermite) and OpenWebText validation loss (from 2.957 to 2.912) are modest and evaluated on a single seed without reporting standard deviations across multiple runs.
Incomplete draft artifacts: There are unfinished sentences and missing links in the manuscript, notably at the end of Section 1 ('...pure PyTorch:') and Footnote 2 on page 7 ('...is available at:').

strengths: Principled initialization approach: The derivation of variance-preserving forward and backward gains for Hermite and Fourier bases using their orthonormality properties is mathematically sound and provides a clean closed-form solution to the second-moment calculus.

Evaluation beyond toy benchmarks: Unlike many recent works on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) and learnable basis activations that evaluate only on toy or low-dimensional datasets (e.g., MNIST, synthetic 1D/2D regressions), this paper tests on standard deep learning benchmarks: ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1K and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText.

Comprehensive ablations: The empirical analysis includes ablations evaluating the effect of basis degree, initialization strategy (derived vs. fitting GELU), and whether coefficients are learnable vs. fixed.
weaknesses: Overstated theoretical contributions: Proposition 3.32 ('Deep Polynomially Activated Neural Networks are Multivariate Polynomial Mappings') is highlighted as one of the paper's core theoretical contributions in the introduction. However, the composition of affine transformations and univariate polynomials is trivially a multivariate polynomial mapping; presenting this well-known, elementary algebraic fact as a formal theoretical novelty is an overstatement.

Incomplete and disjoint treatment of tropical activations: While Hermite and Fourier activations have derived variance-preserving initializations, the tropical polynomial activation is included without any theoretical variance derivation (Remark 3.29 explicitly postpones this to future work and falls back to an ad-hoc 'all ones' initialization). This undermines the cohesive narrative of variance-preserving initialization.

Lack of wall-clock latency, throughput, and memory benchmarking: Learnable basis activations inherently suffer from memory bandwidth and kernel invocation overhead compared to standard pointwise activations like GELU or ReLU. Although Section 4.3 discusses algorithmic complexity and mentions custom CUDA kernels, the paper does not report any empirical wall-clock training throughput (tokens/sec or images/sec), inference latency, or peak GPU memory usage.

Marginal empirical improvements without statistical validation: On ImageNet-1K (Table 1), Hermite activation improves top-1 accuracy by only 0.30% over the GELU baseline, while Fourier activation actually underperforms the baseline (-0.13%). On GPT-2 (Table 2), perplexity drops from 19.24 to 18.39 for Hermite. Without error bars, multiple random seeds, or statistical significance tests, it is unclear whether these narrow improvements are meaningful or merely noise.

Unaddressed distributional drift: The variance-preserving initialization relies on the strong assumption that inputs and gradients remain standard normal or uniformly distributed across all layers. In practice, polynomial transformations alter the higher moments (skewness and kurtosis) of the activations, which can lead to distribution collapse or explosion as depth increases unless strictly constrained (which is why Hermite degree had to be capped at 3).
Formatting and presentation gaps: Several links and citations are incomplete, including an unfinished sentence in the abstract ('pure PyTorch:') and a dangling URL in Footnote 2 ('available at:').

strengths: Principled mathematical foundation: The paper leverages the orthogonality of Hermite polynomials under the Gaussian measure and Fourier bases under the uniform distribution to derive clean, closed-form variance-preserving initializations (matching both forward and backward gains), addressing the historical instability of polynomial activations without ad-hoc clamping or bounding.

Meaningful empirical validation: Unlike many works on exotic or learnable activations that evaluate solely on small benchmarks like MNIST or toy ODEs, this work tests the proposed activations on competitive, large-scale setups, including ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText.

Thoughtful algorithmic and numerical considerations: The authors design an O(d) recurrence relation and dedicated CUDA kernels for Hermite forward/backward passes to reduce computational and memory overhead, and discuss Hermite interpolation (matching derivatives) when transferring from pre-trained activations.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements: The actual performance gains over standard fixed activations (GELU) are modest. On ImageNet-1k (Table 1), Hermite achieves 82.18% vs. 82.01% for GELU (with overlapping confidence bounds given std ~0.13%), and Fourier actually degrades to 81.82%. On GPT-2, the validation perplexity improves marginally (18.80 vs. 19.25).

Computational overhead during training: As noted in Section 6, training is 30% to 90% slower on GPUs compared to standard activations. Given the marginal accuracy gains, the compute-to-accuracy tradeoff may not be practical for general adoption without further specialized kernel optimization.

Overstatement of elementary theoretical results: Highlighting Proposition F.3 ('proving that polynomially activated neural networks are multivariate polynomial mappings') as a primary contribution is an overstatement; the composition of affine maps and univariate polynomials of degree d trivially results in a multivariate polynomial of degree at most d^L, a well-known fact in algebraic machine learning.

Missing comparisons with contemporary adaptive/learnable activation baselines: While the paper extensively reviews and discusses Padé Activation Units (PAU / Molina et al.), KANs, and other learnable activations, experimental comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 are restricted solely to static activations (GELU and SiLU).

strengths: Principled and elegant variance-preserving initialization: The paper derives closed-form initialization conditions for orthogonal basis activations (Hermite polynomials under Gaussian distribution and Fourier series under uniform distribution) ensuring unit forward and backward gains, addressing the long-standing instability of polynomial activations without requiring ad-hoc bounding mechanisms (e.g., SoftSign, explicit clamping).

Empirical validation on non-trivial modern architectures: Unlike many existing works on polynomial or KAN-related activations that only test on toy datasets or shallow MLPs, this work validates Hermite, Fourier, and Tropical activations on ConvNeXt-T (ImageNet-1k) and GPT-2 (OpenWebText) from scratch.

Practical implementation considerations: The authors provide custom algorithms and CUDA implementations leveraging the recurrence relation for Hermite polynomials, bringing the forward/backward complexity down to O(d) in FLOPs and memory.
Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper ablates polynomial degree, initialization scheme (derived gain vs. GELU fit), and parameter learnability, clearly demonstrating the role of each component.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical performance gains: On ImageNet-1k, ConvNeXt-T with Hermite-3 achieves 82.18% Top-1 vs. 82.01% for GELU (a modest +0.17% gain with error bars of ±0.13%), while Fourier-6 actually underperforms GELU (81.82%). Similarly, the validation loss reduction on GPT-2 is relatively small (~0.02 nats).

Significant training latency overhead: As acknowledged in the limitations, training is 30% to 90% slower on GPU compared to standard activations. Given the marginal gains in accuracy/loss, this computational overhead poses a substantial barrier to practical adoption.

Overstated novelty for Proposition F.3: Listing the proof that 'polynomially activated neural networks are multivariate polynomial mappings' as a primary contribution in the introduction and Section F overstates a well-known, elementary mathematical fact (the composition of affine maps and degree-d polynomials is inherently a polynomial of degree at most d^L, widely recognized in prior literature such as Kileel et al., 2019 and Livni et al., 2014).

Limited evaluation of mixed-precision / FP16 stability: Polynomial functions can lead to large magnitude outputs outside the unit variance regime, especially at higher degrees. The paper does not thoroughly discuss numerical stability under standard FP16/BF16 training routines commonly used in large-scale deep learning.

Evaluation in the transfer learning setup (Section 4.5 / Appendix O) freezes all weights except the head and learnable activations. Comparing this solely against a static GELU (which only tunes the linear head) gives an unfair capacity advantage; comparison with standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines (e.g., low-rank adapters or bias tuning) would make the evaluation much more compelling.

strengths: Principled initialization scheme: The derivation of variance-preserving initializations (matching forward and backward second-order moments) for orthogonal function bases (Hermite polynomials and Fourier series) provides a mathematically grounded approach to stabilizing the training of polynomial/basis-based activations without requiring ad-hoc clipping or auxiliary bounding functions.

Evaluation on non-trivial modern architectures: Unlike many related works on polynomial activations or Kolmogorov-Arnold networks that restrict evaluations to toy regression or MNIST/CIFAR datasets, this paper benchmarks on ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText.

Careful numerical and practical implementation: The authors address potential computational bottlenecks by introducing recursive formulations and custom CUDA kernels to keep FLOP and memory complexity linear with respect to the degree.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements vs. high computational overhead: The performance benefits over standard static activations (GELU, SiLU) are very modest (e.g., ImageNet Top-1 moves from 82.01% to 82.18% with Hermite-3, while Fourier-6 degrades to 81.82%; GPT-2 validation loss changes marginally from 2.957 to 2.934). Given that training is reported to be 30% to 90% slower on GPU, the practical utility and cost-benefit trade-off remain questionable.

Overstated theoretical novelty regarding polynomial mappings: Proposition F.3 and the abstract/introduction emphasize as a key contribution that deep polynomially activated neural networks are multivariate polynomial mappings. The fact that the composition of affine maps and polynomial activations yields a polynomial mapping is an elementary algebraic fact well known in the literature (e.g., Kileel et al., 2019; Chrysos et al., 2020), and presenting it as a core result overstates the theoretical novelty.

Brittleness of distributional assumptions: The variance-preserving derivations strictly assume that layer inputs and backpropagated gradients are standard normal $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ (for Hermite) or uniformly distributed (for Fourier). In deep architectures with normalization layers, residual connections, and non-stationary feature distributions throughout training, these assumptions are often violated, leaving the actual variance preservation unverified empirically across training epochs.

Missing comparisons against adaptive/learnable baselines: The experimental evaluation compares the proposed bases almost exclusively against static activations (GELU and SiLU). To properly assess the merit of orthogonal bases, comparisons against existing learnable activation baselines (such as Padé Activation Units, Spline/B-spline activations, or rational activations) under identical training budgets would be necessary.
